summary.title: The Evolution of SRE at Google
summary.one_liner: Google SRE argues that traditional reliability methods (SLOs, error budgets, linear causal chains) are insufficient for complex systems and shows how the STAMP framework, with STPA and CAST, finds hazards and unsafe control actions before outages happen.
keywords: causal analysis based on systems theory
how to find hazards in complex systems
takeaways: Linear chain-of-failures causality models have limits; accidents are better viewed as unsafe interactions between components that each work as designed.
STAMP treats safety as a control problem and models the system-level hazard states that can persist for long periods before an accident.
STPA finds unsafe control actions by classifying them into four types and then enumerates scenarios, including feedback-path failures.
A 2021 Google case study of a quota rightsizer that reduced quota based on wrong usage feedback shows how STPA reveals issues in the feedback path.
Google reports that STPA on complex systems, at a cost of engineer-weeks per analysis, found hundreds of scenarios before they caused outages.
summary.summary: The article, by Google SRE, explains why error budgets and component-level SLOs struggle with zero-loss requirements such as privacy, data loss and compliance in highly complex systems. It introduces Nancy Leveson's STAMP framework and its tools STPA (hazard analysis) and CAST (post-incident analysis), grounded in control theory and Ashby's four conditions for control. A 2021 quota rightsizer incident is used as a worked example to show unsafe control actions, feedback-path failures, and a hazard state that persisted for weeks before an outage. The authors argue system-theoretic methods are the future of SRE, though the results are reported qualitatively.
